Pregnancy

Ozone therapy during pregnancy: claims, uncertainty and risks

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

If back pain, joint pain or another persistent problem is making pregnancy difficult, a treatment described as natural or oxygen-based may sound appealing. Ozone therapy is advertised for a wide range of conditions, but it is not ordinary oxygen treatment, and its benefits and safety in pregnancy have not been established. Do not start an elective ozone treatment during pregnancy on the strength of a clinic’s general promises. Discuss the condition you want treated with your maternity team or an appropriate specialist. If you have already had a session, that does not prove that your baby has been harmed; it is a reason to obtain an individual assessment and record exactly what was used.

Ozone is different from the oxygen used in medical care

Ozone is a molecule made of three oxygen atoms, written O3. The oxygen normally used to support breathing is O2. The difference matters: a substance can contain oxygen atoms without being safe to breathe, inject or use as a substitute for prescribed oxygen.

High in the atmosphere, the ozone layer helps protect Earth from ultraviolet radiation. Near the ground, ozone is an air pollutant. Breathing it can irritate the throat and airways, cause coughing or painful breathing, and worsen asthma. Longer or greater exposure can cause more serious respiratory effects.

The word medical on an ozone product does not remove these properties. Hyperbaric oxygen, in which oxygen is given in a specialist pressure chamber for selected medical indications, is also a different treatment. Similar names should not be used to imply interchangeable evidence or risks.

What an ozone treatment may involve

Ozone therapy is an umbrella term rather than one standard procedure. A provider may mean gas delivered around or into a tissue, an oxygen–ozone mixture used for a joint or spinal problem, a topical product, an ozonated liquid, or a procedure in which blood is taken out, exposed to ozone and returned. These methods expose the body in different ways.

Direct injection of gas into a blood vessel is particularly dangerous because gas can obstruct circulation. A clinic’s statement that it uses another route does not establish that the procedure is effective or safe during pregnancy. Sterility, equipment, the treatment site and the person’s condition also matter.

Ozone has been used for disinfection and proposed medical treatments for more than a century. A long history, a treatment being available locally or a practitioner offering it is not the same as reliable evidence of a favourable benefit–risk balance. Ask what the actual procedure is rather than accepting ozone therapy as a complete description.

Claims about pain, infection and chronic illness

For pain and inflammation, promotional claims include relief from rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, a herniated spinal disc, back pain and neck pain. These are different conditions, so improvement reported for one setting cannot simply be extended to all of them or to pregnant patients.

For infection and tissue healing, claims include killing bacteria, viruses and fungi, disinfecting wounds, preventing wound infection and speeding healing. Ozone has also been promoted against HIV and hepatitis. A laboratory effect on a microorganism does not establish that exposing a person to ozone safely treats that infection.

Other advertised uses include stimulating the immune system, producing antioxidant or anti-inflammatory effects, supporting cancer treatment, controlling diabetes or its complications, and treating narrowed arteries or other cardiovascular problems. Claims about breathing disorders sometimes promise to increase oxygen in the body. Those statements should not be read as established indications or as reasons to replace effective treatment.

If you have one of these conditions, ask for evidence about that particular diagnosis and the exact proposed method. A list of many unrelated benefits is not a substitute for evidence that the treatment helps people in your situation.

Why a possible mechanism is not proof of benefit

Researchers have proposed biological explanations for ozone’s effects, including changes in oxidative stress and inflammatory signalling. Showing a change in a laboratory marker is different from showing that people feel better, avoid complications or live longer. A substance that can damage microbes outside the body may also damage human tissue.

A 2026 umbrella review examined seven meta-analyses across four indications: periodontitis, COVID-19, diabetic foot ulcers and third-molar surgery. Findings were inconsistent, evidence certainty was low or very low, and adverse-event reporting did not allow firm safety conclusions. This was not a pregnancy study and did not evaluate every condition for which ozone is advertised.

Small studies, different treatment methods and incomplete follow-up make confident general promises difficult. Equally, the limits of evidence should be described accurately: uncertainty about a proposed benefit is not proof that every person will be harmed. The practical issue is whether a sufficiently supported benefit justifies the known and unknown risks.

What is known about use during pregnancy

Pregnancy adds questions about the developing baby as well as the person receiving treatment. Reliable pregnancy-specific evidence is insufficient to establish a safe method, dose, trimester or expected benefit. Reassuring reports from nonpregnant adults cannot settle those questions.

For someone considering ozone injections for a painful back, a disc problem or inflamed joints, that uncertainty is a reason to avoid elective treatment and discuss alternatives with their care team. Do not assume that using a smaller amount, a different route or a later stage of pregnancy makes it safe.

Evidence is also insufficient during breastfeeding. That does not create a universal instruction to stop breastfeeding after any exposure; it means the actual procedure and the parent’s and baby’s circumstances need professional assessment. Absence of a recognised problem in a few reports is not the same as a reliable safety study.

How to understand the FDA warning

The US Food and Drug Administration places restrictions on ozone-generating devices. Its device-labelling guidance links to 21 CFR 801.415 and explains that use for a medical condition without proof of safety or effectiveness is not permitted under that provision.

This regulatory context should not be presented as a newly discovered 2019 pregnancy study or a statement that every country has identical rules. Nor does a device being sold or a clinic claiming regulatory compliance amount to proof that its proposed treatment is appropriate for a pregnant patient.

For your decision, the relevant questions remain clinical as well as regulatory: what benefit has been shown, what harms have been examined, and do those data include pregnancy? A clinic should be able to answer clearly without relying only on a product name, professional association or testimonial.

Side effects depend on how ozone is given

Breathing ozone can irritate the eyes, nose, throat and lungs, with coughing, chest discomfort, wheezing or breathing difficulty. Headache, dizziness, nausea and vomiting have also been described around exposures or treatments, but they are not specific to ozone and should not be dismissed as proof that a treatment is working.

Procedures involving needles can cause local pain, bruising or swelling and introduce infection. Flu-like symptoms and muscle aches have been reported after some treatments; reliable frequencies and pregnancy-specific risks are not established. Risks cannot be combined into one simple percentage when the routes and procedures differ.

Serious complications have also been reported. A 2024 case described cerebral gas embolism and stroke during an oxygen–ozone injection for a spinal-disc problem. A 2026 case described sudden weakness and loss of vision after intravenous ozone therapy. Individual reports demonstrate possible serious hazards; they do not measure how commonly these events occur or quantify fetal risk.

If you already had a treatment

Contact your maternity clinician and the treating service for a written record of the date, route, treatment site, substances used and any symptoms. Tell your clinician how far along the pregnancy was, or whether you are breastfeeding. Do not rely on a general online statement to decide what follow-up is necessary.

Get emergency help for breathing difficulty, chest pain, collapse, seizure, sudden weakness, new speech difficulty or loss of vision after a procedure. Explain that ozone or an oxygen–ozone mixture was involved. Urgent symptoms need assessment even if a provider calls them a detoxification reaction.

If you feel well, still seek individual advice rather than assuming either that nothing needs discussing or that harm is certain. The available evidence does not support predicting a baby’s outcome from the treatment name alone. Avoid further sessions while the exposure and your original condition are being reviewed.

Getting help for the problem you hoped to treat

The symptom that led you to consider treatment deserves attention. For back or joint pain, describe its location, duration and effect on sleep and movement. Your clinician can assess the cause and discuss pregnancy-appropriate movement, physiotherapy, support measures or medicines when suitable.

Pain with new weakness, loss of bladder or bowel control, numbness around the groin, fever or other major changes needs urgent assessment rather than a routine alternative-therapy appointment. During pregnancy, bleeding, severe abdominal pain or reduced baby movements also need prompt maternity advice.

For a wound, infection, diabetes, cancer or cardiovascular condition, continue care with the relevant clinical team. Do not delay proven treatment while trying an unestablished therapy. A useful consultation should leave you with a plan for the actual problem, not simply a warning against one advertised option.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Ozone and prescribed oxygen are different substances and treatments. Inhaled ozone is a recognised respiratory hazard.

Available reviews do not establish pregnancy safety; a 2026 umbrella review covered only four nonpregnancy indications and found low or very-low-certainty evidence.

Device restrictions and case reports provide important context, but neither supplies an individual fetal-risk estimate.

How BeMama can help

Before agreeing to a procedure, write down the problem you want help with and ask which options have evidence for your stage of pregnancy. If you have already had treatment, bring the procedure record to your maternity team.

When to seek help

Avoid elective ozone therapy in pregnancy. Serious respiratory, chest or neurological symptoms after a procedure require emergency assessment. Previous exposure does not, by itself, prove fetal harm.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Ozone therapy is not ordinary oxygen treatment.
  • Claims for many conditions do not establish pregnancy benefit or safety.
  • The route matters; direct vascular gas exposure and other procedures can cause serious harm.
  • No reliable safe pregnancy dose or trimester has been established.
  • If already exposed, obtain an individual assessment rather than assuming a particular outcome.

Frequently asked questions

Is ozone safe because it contains oxygen?

No. Ozone has three oxygen atoms and different chemical properties from the oxygen used to support breathing. Its name does not establish safety.

Can it treat back or joint pain during pregnancy?

Pregnancy-specific benefit and safety have not been established. Avoid starting an elective ozone procedure and ask your maternity team or specialist about appropriate assessment and alternatives.

Does killing germs in a laboratory mean it treats HIV or hepatitis?

No. A laboratory disinfectant effect does not prove a safe and effective treatment inside a person. Continue specialist care and do not substitute ozone for established infection treatment.

Is a topical treatment automatically safer than an injection?

Different routes have different hazards, but that does not establish pregnancy safety for a topical or liquid product. The exact preparation, use and evidence would still need assessment.

Has ozone therapy been banned everywhere?

Rules differ by jurisdiction. The US FDA guidance cited here describes restrictions on ozone devices; it is not proof of a worldwide legal rule or a pregnancy-specific authorisation.

Does a small dose or later trimester make it safe?

There is no reliable evidence establishing a safe pregnancy dose, route or trimester. Those changes should not be used as reassurance without appropriate evidence and clinical advice.

Have I harmed my baby if I already had one session?

That cannot be concluded from the treatment name alone. Contact your maternity clinician with the date and procedure details so that your circumstances and any symptoms can be assessed.

Are headaches or flu-like symptoms a healthy detox reaction?

They should not be assumed to be beneficial. New symptoms after a procedure warrant advice, and severe breathing, chest or neurological symptoms require emergency care.

Is ozone therapy the same as hyperbaric oxygen?

No. Hyperbaric oxygen is a distinct specialist treatment. Evidence for one cannot be transferred to the other simply because both names involve oxygen.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
